passage: Three days before the school assembly in their Pune colony school, Usha's speech on water shortage was a wall of facts. She read it to her friend Nikita on the terrace, and Nikita's eyes drifted to the kites. "You lost me at the second number," Nikita admitted. Usha was stung, but she tried again. This time she started with a question: "Who here had a bucket bath this morning because the tank was empty?" Then three points, one story about her building's tanker, and a closing line. On the day, her knees shook and her mouth went dry. She held the mic stand, found Nikita's face in the third row, and asked her question. Half the hall raised their hands. Someone laughed. Usha relaxed a little and kept going.

qa.q: What question did Usha open her speech with?
qa.a: She asked who had a bucket bath that morning because the tank was empty.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when Nikita said, "You lost me at the second number"?
qa.a: She felt stung and a bit hurt, but she took it as a sign the speech was not working and chose to fix it.

qa.q: What helped Usha keep going when her knees shook?
qa.a: Holding the mic stand, finding a friendly face and starting with a question that got hands up gave her something steady and made the audience part of the talk.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel sitting in the third row during the speech?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and a little responsible, since her honest comment helped Usha change the opening that now held the hall.

grounding: It shows a teen restructuring a talk around a question and story, managing stage fear and holding the audience's attention.

passage:
"Didi, you're talking to the wall again."
"I'm practising, Sachin. Go away."
"Why are you whispering, though? The hall is huge."
Disha lowered her notes. "Because if I say it loud and mess up, it's real."
"Say it to me. I'm eleven. I don't count."
She sighed and started. "Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about—" She stopped. "My voice is shaking."
"So? Mine shakes when I ask Papa for money."
She laughed despite herself. "Okay. Again."
"Slower. And look at me, not the paper."
"Since when are you a coach?"
"Since you started whispering at walls."
The third time, she got through the first minute without looking down. Sachin clapped with his feet on the sofa. "Now do it louder."

qa.q: How old does Sachin say he is?
qa.a: He says he is eleven.

qa.q: Why was Disha whispering her speech?
qa.a: She was afraid that saying it loudly and making a mistake would make her failure feel real, so whispering felt safer.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's tips helped, and why?
qa.a: Telling her to go slower and look at him instead of the paper gave her a real listener, so she got through the first minute without looking down.

qa.q: What is it like for Sachin to coach his older sister?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy it and feel useful, teasing her while also cheering her on by clapping. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teen practising a speech at home, facing stage fear with a sibling's help and building delivery.

passage: Last year I was picked to speak at the district science fair, and I nearly said no. I'm Imran, and until then I had never spoken to more than my own class. My plan was to memorise everything. On the day, the first sentence came out and then my mind went blank. I stood there, hearing the fan. Sangeeta Ma'am, our physics teacher, was holding up my cue card from the front row. I read one word, "magnets," and the rest came back. Later she told me people remember stories more than scripts. So this year I built the talk on three cards: the problem, what we tried, the moment it failed. My hands were still cold. But I looked up more, and people actually laughed at the failure part.

qa.q: What was the one word Imran read from the cue card?
qa.a: He read the word "magnets."

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when his mind went blank?
qa.a: He was frozen with fear, standing silent and hearing only the fan, as if the memorised script had vanished.

qa.q: What changed in how Imran prepared this year, and why did it help?
qa.a: He built the talk on three cards around a story instead of memorising a script, so one cue could bring back the whole flow.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Ma'am have felt holding up the card in the front row?
qa.a: She was probably anxious for Imran but ready to help, and then glad when one word got him going again.

grounding: A teen looks back on freezing during a talk and learning to structure speeches around cues and a story.

passage: It was the night before Urmila's history test, and the power kept cutting out. Each time the lights came back, she grabbed her phone instead of her book. Just one video. A dance clip, then a funny cat, then a clip about "five signs your friends secretly hate you." She hadn't searched for any of it. At 11 pm her cousin Wasim came in for the charger. "Still on chapter four?" he asked. She showed him the feed. "How does it know what I like?" Wasim shrugged. "It watches how long you stop on each one. The longer you stay, the more money they make." Urmila felt a bit sick, like she'd been tricked. She turned off autoplay, put the phone in the next room, and lit a candle for the book.

qa.q: What time was it when Wasim came in for the charger?
qa.a: It was 11 pm.

qa.q: Why did Urmila feel a bit sick after Wasim's explanation?
qa.a: She realised the feed had been choosing clips to hold her attention, so she felt tricked and uneasy about how much time she had lost.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's steps is most likely to help, and why?
qa.a: Putting the phone in the next room works best, because it removes the easy grab each time the lights come back, while turning off autoplay also breaks the chain of clips.

qa.q: What would change if Urmila had not heard Wasim's explanation?
qa.a: She might have kept blaming herself or kept scrolling, without understanding that the feed is built to keep her watching.

grounding: It shows a teen realising, during power cuts before a test, that her feed was designed to keep her engaged.

passage: On the Metro in Delhi, Shalini watched her friend Himani scroll with her thumb moving on its own. Double-tap, swipe, double-tap. "Why do you like everything?" Shalini asked. "So they like mine back," Himani said without looking up. Then her phone buzzed: 43 likes on her new photo. Her face lit up. Ten minutes later it buzzed again, 44, and she checked instantly. Shalini frowned. "It's like a slot machine. You never know when the next one comes, so you keep checking." Himani laughed, then stopped. "That's actually creepy." At their stop she turned off the like alerts in settings. Her hand still went to the phone twice on the stairs. "Habit," she muttered, embarrassed.

qa.q: How many likes did Himani's photo have when her phone first buzzed?
qa.a: It had 43 likes.

qa.q: What does Himani's hand going to the phone twice on the stairs suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the checking had become an automatic habit, and her muttered "Habit" shows she feels a little embarrassed noticing it.

qa.q: What else could Himani try besides turning off like alerts?
qa.a: She could keep the phone in her bag during trips and set specific times to check, so the unpredictable buzz loses its pull.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel watching Himani on the Metro?
qa.a: She might feel worried and a bit left out, since Himani's attention is on the likes and not on their conversation.

grounding: It shows teens noticing how likes and alerts are designed like unpredictable rewards to keep users checking.

passage:
"Jeevan, it's one in the morning."
"One more, Ma. It's a short one."
"You said that at midnight."
"They're all short! That's the thing."
Gopika Aunty sat on the edge of his bed. "Tell me what you watched first."
"A football goal."
"And now?"
Jeevan looked. "Some man shouting about why everyone's wrong about everything." He frowned. "How did I get here?"
"You tell me."
"Each video... it picks the next one. Something a bit more exciting than the last, I think."
"So who's deciding what you watch?"
He was quiet. "Not me, I guess." He felt annoyed, but not really at her. He put the phone face down. "Can we move the charger to the hall?"
"Your idea, not mine," she said, smiling.

qa.q: What was the first video Jeevan watched?
qa.a: He watched a football goal.

qa.q: What made Jeevan feel annoyed, and at whom?
qa.a: He was annoyed at realising the feed had pulled him from a goal to a shouting man without him choosing, so the irritation was at the feed and himself rather than his mother.

qa.q: How did Gopika Aunty help Jeevan see the problem?
qa.a: She asked questions instead of lecturing, so he traced the path himself and came up with moving the charger as his own idea.

qa.q: What would change if Gopika Aunty had just taken the phone away?
qa.a: Jeevan might have felt punished and argued, and he would not have understood how the recommendations kept leading him on.

grounding: It shows a parent helping a teen notice how recommendations chain videos to keep him watching late at night.

passage: In the kasba, everybody knew everybody, so when Kavitha posted a video mocking the new maths teacher's accent, it was round the whole school by lunch. She deleted it that evening. Her cousin Sunaina, home from college, showed her a screenshot on her own phone. "Someone saved it. It's in four groups already." Kavitha's stomach dropped. "But I deleted it." "Deleting only removes your copy," Sunaina said gently. The next week, the teacher was quieter in class, and Kavitha couldn't look at her. Her father, who ran the photocopy shop, had heard about it from a customer. Kavitha went to the teacher after school and apologised, her voice shaking. She didn't know if the teacher forgave her. She stopped posting for a while.

qa.q: How many groups had Kavitha's video reached according to Sunaina?
qa.a: It had reached four groups already.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha's stomach drop when she saw the screenshot?
qa.a: She realised deleting the video had not erased it, and that her joke was now out of her control and hurting the teacher and her own name.

qa.q: What was wise about Kavitha's response after she learned the video had spread?
qa.a: She apologised to the teacher in person instead of hiding, which took responsibility even though she could not undo the posts.

qa.q: How might the maths teacher feel after the video spread?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and self-conscious, since she became quieter in class, and she may take time to trust the students again.

grounding: It shows a teen learning that a deleted post had already been saved and shared, affecting her reputation and another person.

passage: Oskar was sixteen and applying for a summer job at the café near his flat in Gothenburg. The owner, a friendly woman with flour on her sleeves, said, "I looked you up, of course." Oskar went pale. His friend Xin was waiting outside, and after the interview Oskar grabbed her arm. "What did she see?" They searched his name together. The first things: a school football photo, a comment he'd written at thirteen calling a referee an idiot, and a silly video of him falling off a bench. "The comment's the worst," Xin said. Oskar winced. "I was thirteen!" "It doesn't say that on it." That night he went through his old accounts, removing what he could and making others private. He still got the job.

qa.q: Where was the café Oskar applied to?
qa.a: It was near his flat in Gothenburg.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling when the owner said she had looked him up?
qa.a: He was suddenly worried and embarrassed, afraid she had seen old posts he no longer wanted linked to him.

qa.q: What could Oskar do from now on to protect his online reputation?
qa.a: He could pause before posting and ask whether he'd be fine with a future employer or teacher seeing it.

qa.q: How does Xin see Oskar's old comment?
qa.a: She sees it as the worst item because, without his age attached, it looks like the current Oskar being rude, not a younger boy.

grounding: It shows a teen discovering that old comments and photos persist online and shape how others see him.

passage: The school's computer lab had a poster that said "Think before you post," and nobody read it. Then, during the careers fair, a college recruiter showed the Class 11 students a slide of anonymous posts from applicants: a rude joke, a photo mocking a classmate, a fight in a comment section. "These are real," he said. "Some were years old." Hansa glanced at Rafiq. He had shared a meme about a girl in their class last month. Rafiq stared at his shoes. After the session, he pulled out his phone in the corridor. "Help me find it," he muttered. They found the meme had been shared by eleven other people. He deleted his, then messaged the girl to say sorry. Hansa noticed his hands shaking as he typed.

qa.q: How many other people had shared Rafiq's meme?
qa.a: Eleven other people had shared it.

qa.q: What does Rafiq staring at his shoes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and uneasy, because the recruiter's slides reminded him of the meme he had shared about a classmate.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on the recruiter's talk for students like Rafiq?
qa.a: The teacher could give time to review their own accounts and discuss how to repair harm, like apologising, not just deleting.

qa.q: How might the girl in the meme feel when she gets Rafiq's apology?
qa.a: She might feel relieved that he admitted it, though still hurt that the meme had spread so widely.

grounding: It shows teens realising that posts spread and persist and can affect future chances and other people.

subtype: Using AI Tools Ethically & Verifying Outputs
passage: Tanvir's village had one good internet spot near the water tank, and that's where he sat with his cousin Binita, typing questions into an AI chat tool for his Class 10 project on local crops. "Ask it to write the whole thing," Binita whispered. It was tempting. The answer came back fast, neat, and full of facts, including a citation to a government report. Tanvir frowned. "It says millets grow best in flooded fields. That's wrong. Abba grows them on the dry side." They tried to find the report. It didn't exist. Binita's grin faded. Tanvir used the tool to make a list of questions instead, then walked to the farm office to ask the officer himself. His project was shorter, but every line was his own.

qa.q: Where was the good internet spot in Tanvir's village?
qa.a: It was near the water tank.

qa.q: Why did Binita's grin fade?
qa.a: She realised the tool had given a wrong fact and a report that did not exist, so copying it would have been embarrassing and dishonest.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do well in using the AI tool?
qa.a: He used it to plan questions, checked its claims against his father's farming and the real report, and wrote the project himself.

qa.q: How might the farm officer see Tanvir's visit?
qa.a: He might be pleased that a student came with real questions and cared about getting local facts right.

grounding: It shows a teen catching an AI tool's false claim and fake citation and using it for learning rather than outsourcing.

subtype: Using AI Tools Ethically & Verifying Outputs
passage: Kwame had an essay due on the history of the Gold Coast, and it was nearly midnight in Accra. His sister Esther, home from university, found him with an AI tool open and a finished essay on the screen. "You wrote that in ten minutes?" she asked. He shrugged, a bit guilty. "Read me the second paragraph." He did. "Who's that historian?" she asked. He checked. The name led nowhere. "And that date is wrong. I did this for my exams." Kwame groaned. "So I have to start again?" "Use it to explain what confuses you," Esther said. "Then check the facts in your textbook and write it yourself." He grumbled, but by one o'clock he had a messy, honest first draft.

qa.q: What time was it when Esther found Kwame with the essay?
qa.a: It was nearly midnight.

qa.q: How can you tell Kwame felt guilty about the essay?
qa.a: He shrugged a bit guiltily when Esther asked if he wrote it in ten minutes, suggesting he knew he hadn't really done the work.

qa.q: What advice did Esther give, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She told him to use the tool to explain confusing parts, then check facts and write it himself, so he learns and avoids false claims.

qa.q: How might Kwame's teacher react if he had submitted the first essay?
qa.a: The teacher might have spotted the fake historian and wrong date, and then doubted Kwame's honesty and understanding.

grounding: It shows a teen learning to check an AI tool's citations and use it for understanding rather than writing for him.

subtype: Using AI Tools Ethically & Verifying Outputs
passage: In the Class 12 computer lab, the teacher allowed AI tools for one hour of project work, with a rule: every fact had to be checked against a second source. Jaya asked hers to summarise a chapter on climate. Her friend Ankita asked hers for five references. Ankita was done in five minutes and grinning. Jaya was still reading. "Just copy it," Ankita said. Jaya shook her head and clicked the first reference. It took her to a real journal, but the article said something different. The second link didn't open at all. Ankita checked hers and went quiet; two of her five were made up. She sighed. "So it lies?" "It guesses," Jaya said. "Confidently." They spent the rest of the hour hunting for real sources.

qa.q: What rule did the teacher set for using AI tools?
qa.a: Every fact had to be checked against a second source.

qa.q: What does Ankita going quiet suggest when she checks her references?
qa.a: It suggests she was surprised and a bit uneasy to find two made-up references after feeling confident she was done.

qa.q: Why did the teacher's rule matter?
qa.a: It forced students to verify claims, which exposed the made-up and misquoted references before they could spoil the projects.

qa.q: How might Ankita see AI tools differently after this lesson?
qa.a: She will probably see them as helpful but unreliable, something to check rather than trust just because the answer sounds sure.

grounding: It shows teens in a school lab finding that AI-generated references can be false and must be checked.

passage:
Monday: Jomon, fifteen, got a message on a gaming chat from someone called "Riya" who said she was sixteen and lived nearby. She was funny and knew all his favourite players. Jomon felt flattered.

Thursday: "Riya" asked for a photo, then a more private one. When he said no, the tone changed: "Send it or I'll tell everyone what you said." Jomon's hands went cold. He didn't sleep. He almost sent it just to make it stop.

Saturday: He told his older sister Tanuja, shaking. She didn't shout. She helped him take screenshots, block the account and report it. Then they told their parents together, who went with him to the cyber cell. Jomon cried with relief when the officer said, "You did the right thing."

qa.q: Who did Jomon tell on Saturday?
qa.a: He told his older sister Tanuja.

qa.q: Why did Jomon almost send the photo?
qa.a: He was frightened by the threat and exhausted from not sleeping, so giving in felt like the only way to make the pressure stop.

qa.q: What made Tanuja's response helpful?
qa.a: She stayed calm, helped him keep screenshots, block and report the account, and brought in their parents, so he wasn't facing it alone.

qa.q: What would change if Jomon had kept the threat secret?
qa.a: The person could have kept pressuring him, and he would have carried the fear alone without the protection of his family and the police.

grounding: It shows a teen recognising manipulative online contact that turns into blackmail, and reporting it to trusted adults.

passage: Neelam, listen, this happened to my friend Minakshi's son when you were small. A man online said he was a talent scout. He told the boy he could be in advertisements, that he just needed to pay a registration fee and send photos. The boy was so happy he didn't tell anyone. The man kept asking for more money, and then said, "If you tell your parents, the offer is cancelled." That line is what made Minakshi's son stop and think. Why would a real job need secrets? He showed his mother the chat. She called the helpline, and they learned it was a known trick. The money was gone, but the boy was safe. Remember that: real people don't ask you to hide things from your family.

qa.q: What did the man say he was?
qa.a: He said he was a talent scout.

qa.q: What made Minakshi's son suspicious in the end?
qa.a: The demand to keep it secret from his parents made him wonder why a genuine offer would need hiding, so doubt replaced his excitement.

qa.q: What should Neelam do if an online contact asks her to keep secrets?
qa.a: She should treat it as a warning sign, stop replying, keep the messages and tell a parent or trusted adult straight away.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when her son showed her the chat?
qa.a: She was probably shaken that he'd been targeted but relieved he came to her, and glad to act quickly with the helpline. 🙏

grounding: An elder uses a family memory to teach a younger person to recognise a fraud's demand for secrecy and to tell trusted adults.

passage: Deepak had forty minutes before his bus to the coaching centre when the message arrived: "Your account will be blocked today. Click here to verify your bank details." It had his name and the bank's logo. His father's card was linked to Deepak's phone for fees, and panic rose in his chest. He was about to tap the link when his friend Yusuf, waiting with him at the bus stop, leaned over. "Bro, look at the sender. It's a random number." Deepak's thumb froze. "But it says today." "That's the trick. They rush you." Deepak didn't click. He called his father, who checked with the bank from his office. The message was fake. His father reported the number and thanked Yusuf by name that evening.

qa.q: How long did Deepak have before his bus?
qa.a: He had forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did panic rise in Deepak's chest?
qa.a: The message used his name, the logo and a same-day deadline, and his father's card was linked to his phone, so he feared causing a real problem.

qa.q: What is the wise step Deepak took instead of clicking?
qa.a: He called his father so an adult could check directly with the bank, rather than acting on the rushed message.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see the urgent message?
qa.a: He sees the random sender and the "today" deadline as signs of a trick designed to rush people into acting without thinking.

grounding: It shows a teen under time pressure recognising a phishing scam and turning to a trusted adult.

passage:
Dear Imran,
You asked why I've been missing our morning walks. Honestly? I haven't been sleeping. I start a game "for twenty minutes" at ten and look up at two. My eyes feel full of sand in first period. Last week I fell asleep in chemistry and Ma'am had to tap my desk. I was so embarrassed 😔
The weird part is I don't even enjoy the last hours. I'm just stuck doing one more round.
So I'm trying something. The laptop now charges in Mummy's room after ten. I told her myself. I set an alarm at 9:45 as a warning. Tonight was the first try and I was restless, but I slept by eleven.
Walk tomorrow? 6:30, the usual gate.
Ankita

qa.q: Where does Ankita's laptop charge after ten now?
qa.a: It charges in her mother's room.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when she fell asleep in chemistry?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed when her teacher had to tap her desk, which helped her see that the late gaming was causing real trouble.

qa.q: Why might Ankita's plan work better than just promising to stop?
qa.a: Moving the laptop and setting a warning alarm put a physical limit in place, so she doesn't rely on willpower at 10 pm.

qa.q: How might Imran feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He might be relieved to know why she skipped the walks and happy she wants to meet again, and glad she was honest with him.

grounding: It shows a teen noticing that gaming has pushed out sleep and setting her own limits.

passage: So you want to know how bad it got? Okay. I'm Harsha, I'm sixteen, and three months ago I was scrolling till three every night. Not even fun stuff, just scrolling. My sister Minakshi noticed first. She shares my room and said my screen lit up the whole ceiling. I told her to mind her business. But then I failed a test I'd actually studied for, because I couldn't think straight. That scared me. I checked my screen time and it was, like, seven hours a day. I didn't believe it. Now I keep the phone across the room so I have to get up. I still slip sometimes. But I sleep more, and Minakshi says I'm less grumpy in the mornings, which, honestly, rude. But true.

qa.q: Who noticed Harsha's late-night scrolling first?
qa.a: Her sister Minakshi, who shares her room, noticed first.

qa.q: Why did failing the test scare Harsha?
qa.a: She had studied, so failing made her realise the lost sleep was hurting her thinking, not just her mood.

qa.q: What could Harsha add if she keeps slipping some nights?
qa.a: She could set a fixed time to put the phone away each night and maybe ask Minakshi to remind her, without being harsh on herself.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see the change in Harsha?
qa.a: She probably finds the room darker and quieter at night and Harsha easier to be around, and may feel glad she spoke up. 🙂

grounding: A teen describes noticing compulsive scrolling and its effect on sleep and marks, then setting a limit.

passage: I'm Rukmini, and Madhav is the boy next door. We've taken the same school bus since we were small. This year he started sleeping on it, head against the window, mouth open. He missed his stop twice. His mother told mine he gamed with friends online till late, sometimes till the birds started. Last month something shifted. I saw him at the bus stop with a paperback, yawning but awake. He said his friends now log off at eleven together; they made a rule so no one feels left out. He still looked tired on Mondays. Once I heard him tell his little brother, "Phone down, bed. I'm serious." I don't know how hard it was for him, but he hasn't missed his stop since.

qa.q: How many times did Madhav miss his stop?
qa.a: He missed his stop twice.

qa.q: What might Madhav's still-tired Mondays suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he may still slip on weekends, and that keeping the limit is an ongoing effort rather than a finished change.

qa.q: Why did the friends' shared log-off rule work well?
qa.a: Logging off together at eleven meant no one feared missing out, so it was easier for Madhav to stop.

qa.q: How might Madhav's little brother feel being told "Phone down, bed"?
qa.a: He might feel annoyed at being bossed, but he may also sense his brother is serious because he knows how it feels.

grounding: A neighbour observes a teen's gaming cutting into his sleep and the limit he sets with friends.

passage: You asked how it felt, turning fourteen. Okay. I'm Pranav. That year I grew fast, and my arms got long and thin and my voice cracked. My cousin Leela, she's older, showed me photos of some boys online with huge muscles. I started comparing everything. I'd stand sideways in the mirror. I skipped dinner a few times, thinking it would make me look sharper. Then Leela noticed, and she felt terrible, I think. She sat with me and said those photos are edited, posed, lit perfectly. She said my body was still changing and would do its own thing. Our PE teacher said the same, and that if I was worried I could talk to the doctor. I stopped skipping meals. I still stand sideways sometimes. But I laugh at myself now.

qa.q: What did Pranav skip a few times?
qa.a: He skipped dinner a few times.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she noticed Pranav skipping meals?
qa.a: Pranav thinks she felt terrible, likely because the photos she had shown him seemed to have started his comparing.

qa.q: What made the adults' and Leela's responses helpful?
qa.a: They explained that the photos were edited and posed, reminded him his body was still changing, and pointed him to a doctor if worried, without shaming him.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had never noticed?
qa.a: Pranav might have kept skipping meals and comparing himself to edited images, and the harmful habit could have grown quietly.

grounding: A teen describes comparing his changing body to idealised images, starting a harmful habit, and turning towards acceptance with support.

passage: I'm Mridul. Ojas and I have been in the same swimming class since Class 7. This year he started wearing a big T-shirt over his swimsuit, even in the water. Coach asked him to take it off, and Ojas went red and said he was cold. He wasn't. He'd been quiet in the changing room since some older boys joked about the hair on his chest. After that he missed two classes. I didn't really know what to say, so I told him that my shoulders are crooked and I've stopped caring. He laughed a little. Last week he came without the T-shirt. He still turned his back when the older boys walked by. Coach told them off for teasing and changed the lane groups.

qa.q: What did Ojas start wearing over his swimsuit?
qa.a: He started wearing a big T-shirt.

qa.q: Why did Ojas say he was cold when he wasn't?
qa.a: He was embarrassed about his body after the older boys' jokes and needed an excuse to keep covered without explaining.

qa.q: How did the coach help, and what else could he do?
qa.a: He stopped the teasing and changed lane groups; he could also have a private word with Ojas to check how he's feeling.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul to watch this happen?
qa.a: He seems unsure what to say and a bit worried, so he tries sharing his own insecurity to make Ojas feel less alone.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen hiding his changing body after teasing, and gradually regaining some self-acceptance.

passage:
Week one: Urmila deleted her class photo from her profile because her face looked "round." Her friend Kashish commented, "You look nice!" Urmila didn't believe her. She spent the evening comparing herself with a filtered model's pictures.

Week three: In health class, the teacher showed how one photo can be changed with filters and lighting. Urmila felt oddly angry at how much time she'd wasted. She unfollowed several accounts that made her feel worse.

Week six: She and Kashish went cycling on Sunday and laughed so much she forgot about her face. At home she noticed she hadn't opened the mirror app in days. She reposted the class photo. It still felt strange, but she kept it up. 🙂

qa.q: What did the health teacher show the class in week three?
qa.a: The teacher showed how one photo can be changed with filters and lighting.

qa.q: Why did Urmila feel angry after the health class?
qa.a: She realised she had been comparing herself to images that weren't real, and felt upset about the time she had wasted feeling bad.

qa.q: What choices helped Urmila move towards self-acceptance?

passage:
Kashish,
I'm writing this because I can't say it properly out loud. I'm sorry for Saturday. When you asked if I wanted to come to the fair, I snapped "Stop asking me stuff!" and slammed the door. You didn't deserve that.
I don't even know why I was angry. One minute I was fine and then everything felt too loud. It keeps happening this year. Mummy says a lot of it is growing up, and to talk to the doctor if it gets too much, which I might.
What I'm trying now is to say "give me ten minutes" instead of snapping. It worked twice this week.
Can we go to the fair next week instead? I'll buy the candyfloss.
Nikita

qa.q: What did Nikita snap at Kashish?
qa.a: She snapped "Stop asking me stuff!" and slammed the door.

qa.q: What does Nikita mean when she says "everything felt too loud"?
qa.a: She is describing a sudden wave of irritation that she didn't choose and can't fully explain, which confuses her.

qa.q: Why is saying "give me ten minutes" a good step for Nikita?
qa.a: It gives her space to let the mood pass without hurting someone, and tells others what she needs.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She will probably feel relieved and understood, knowing the snap wasn't really about her, and happy about the fair plan. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes an apology showing she understands her sudden moods and is choosing a better way to act.

passage: You're recording? Okay. I'm Kunal. I used to think I was just an angry person. Like, this year my younger cousin Bhupen came to stay, and he's nice, but everything he did annoyed me. The way he chewed. The way he said "bro." I'd feel this heat rising and I'd say something mean. Then later I'd feel awful and not know why I said it. My dad said he was the same at my age and that the moods pass, but I still have to choose what I do. So now when the heat comes, I go to the terrace for a bit. Sometimes I put on music. Bhupen and I actually play carrom now. I still get annoyed by the chewing though. That hasn't changed.

qa.q: Where does Kunal go when the heat rises?
qa.a: He goes to the terrace for a bit.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel after saying something mean to Bhupen?
qa.a: He felt awful and confused about why he'd said it, which shows the anger didn't match how he really felt about his cousin.

qa.q: Why is going to the terrace a useful habit for Kunal?
qa.a: It gives him a pause between the feeling and the action, so the mood can pass without him hurting Bhupen.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Kunal before the change?
qa.a: He probably felt unwelcome and confused, not knowing why his cousin kept snapping at small things like chewing.

grounding: A teen describes sudden irritability and choosing to step away rather than lash out.

passage: My brother Varun turned fifteen in March, and since then I've been living with a weather forecast I can't read. I'm Kavitha, his older sister. Some evenings he tells us jokes at dinner. Other evenings he slams his plate down because the rice is "too wet." Last Tuesday, Mummy asked about his homework, and he shouted. Then, a minute later, he came back from his room. His ears were red. "Sorry," he mumbled. "I'm just... I don't know." He went to fill the water bottles, which is his job, without being asked. I don't know what goes on in his head. But I've noticed he comes back faster now. Mummy says to give him room and not tease. I'm trying, though it's hard.

qa.q: What did Varun complain about the rice?
qa.a: He said it was "too wet."

qa.q: What might Varun's red ears suggest when he came back?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and sorry about shouting, even though he couldn't explain his mood.

qa.q: How could the family support Varun during his mood swings?
qa.a: They could give him space in the moment, as Mummy says, and notice when he chooses to come back and repair things.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha to live with Varun's changing moods?
qa.a: It feels unpredictable and sometimes hard, but she's trying to be patient and notices small improvements.

grounding: A sister observes a teen's sudden irritability and his growing choice to return and repair.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11:
Vinita came to me after a fight at home. She wanted to stay late at a friend's birthday, until eleven. Her mother, Alka, said nine. Vinita said, "You never trust me," and Alka said, "You haven't shown me why I should." Both left upset.
In our session, Vinita realised she had asked in the middle of her mother's cooking, while shouting. We role-played asking calmly, with details: where, who, how she'd get home. She suggested a middle time, ten, with a call at nine. She seemed surprised when I said her mother's worry might come from love, not control.
Follow-up: Vinita reports Alka agreed to ten. She called at nine. She said her mother smiled when she came home on time.

qa.q: What time did Alka finally agree to?
qa.a: She agreed to ten, with a call at nine.

qa.q: Why was Vinita surprised during the session?
qa.a: She had seen her mother's rule as control, so it was new to her that the worry might come from love.

qa.q: What made Vinita's second request more likely to succeed?
qa.a: She asked calmly at a good moment, gave details about where, who and transport, and offered a middle time with a check-in call.

qa.q: How might Alka see Vinita after she came home on time?
qa.a: She likely felt reassured and more willing to trust her, which may make the next request easier.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen learning to negotiate a curfew respectfully and build trust with a parent.

passage:
Friday night
Asked Papa if I could go to the school trip to the hills. Two nights! He said no before I even finished. I went to my room and nearly cried. Neelam texted: "Did u ask nicely or did u do the Reena thing?" The Reena thing = sulking. Rude but fair 😅
So I thought about what scares him. It's the night part, and not knowing the teachers. So I found the trip letter with the teacher's number and the hotel name. I wrote a list: where, who, what time we'd call. I made him tea and gave him the list.
He read it twice. Said "I'll call the teacher." Not a yes. But not a no either. I'm counting that as a win.

qa.q: What did Reena give Papa along with tea?
qa.a: She gave him a list of where, who and what time they would call.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling after Papa's first no?
qa.a: She was upset and nearly cried, feeling dismissed before she could even explain.

qa.q: Which choice in Reena's second try made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Thinking about what scared Papa and giving him the teacher's number and details addressed his worry instead of just arguing.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt reading Reena's list?
qa.a: He probably felt more reassured and saw she was serious and responsible, which is why he agreed to call the teacher.

grounding: It shows a teen negotiating permission for an overnight trip by addressing a parent's worries with respect.

passage:
Before: When the unit test results came, Neelam got 71 in maths. Her friend Harish got 94 and said, "That was easy." At home, her mother asked what Harish got. Neelam lied and said 80. She went to bed feeling small and stupid.

During: The next week, a teacher asked the class to write one thing they had improved since last year. Neelam wrote: "I can do word problems now." It was true. She stared at the sentence for a while.

After: A few days later, she told her mother the real mark. Her mother was quiet, then asked, "Which part was hard?" They made a plan for algebra. Neelam still felt a pinch when Harish talked about marks, but it didn't stay all night.

qa.q: What mark did Neelam get in maths?
qa.a: She got 71.

qa.q: Why did Neelam lie about her mark?
qa.a: She was afraid of being compared with Harish and felt small and stupid, so she wanted to hide the gap from her mother.

qa.q: What helped Neelam's self-worth recover?
qa.a: Writing down a real improvement reminded her of her own progress, and her mother's focus on the hard part turned the talk into a plan instead of a judgement.

qa.q: What would change if her mother had scolded her for the real mark?
qa.a: Neelam might have kept lying and feeling small, and they would not have made a plan for algebra together.

grounding: It shows a teen coping over several days with rank comparison and parental expectations without losing self-worth.

passage: Manjula, sit with me. I want to tell you about your uncle Baljeet when he was your age. He came fifth in the district, and your grandfather asked, "Why not first?" I still remember his face. He stopped eating properly and studied every night till his eyes were red. One day he told me, "If I'm not first, I'm nothing." That scared me. So I took him to the fields where your grandfather grew up and asked him to help pick cotton for a day. He came back tired and laughing. That night, he said, "Bua, maybe fifth isn't nothing." He still worked hard. But he also played cricket again. Beta, marks matter. They're just not who you are.

qa.q: What rank did Baljeet get in the district?
qa.a: He came fifth in the district.

qa.q: What did Baljeet's words, "If I'm not first, I'm nothing," reveal about how he felt?
qa.a: They show he had tied his whole worth to his rank, which made him feel worthless despite doing well.

qa.q: What could Manjula take from Baljeet's story when she feels pressure?
qa.a: She could keep working hard but also make room for things she enjoys, remembering that a mark does not decide her value.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's father have felt if he knew what his question caused?
qa.a: He might have felt sorry, since he likely meant to push Baljeet higher, not make him feel like nothing.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative about someone who coped with rank pressure without losing his sense of worth.

passage: The results went up on the board at nine, and by 9:05 Payal's phone was full of messages. "What did u get??" Her mother had already called twice. Payal had 82%. Her cousin Himani, who studied in the same school, had 91%. Payal's chest tightened. She went to the library, the only quiet place, and sat with her head on the desk. When her mother called a third time, she didn't pick up. Instead she wrote in her notebook: "82 is not a failure. I did better in physics than last year. I'm tired." Then she called back. "82, Ma. I know you hoped for more. I'm okay, and I'd like to talk tonight, not now." Her mother paused. "Okay. Come home, we'll eat."

qa.q: What percentage did Payal have?
qa.a: Payal had 82%.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she sat with her head on the desk?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and anxious, with a tight chest, because of the messages, her mother's calls and the comparison with Himani.

qa.q: What worked in the way Payal handled the pressure?
qa.a: She took a quiet moment, reminded herself of her progress in writing, then called back calmly and asked to talk later.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother have felt when Payal asked to talk later?
qa.a: She may have been disappointed but also reassured by Payal's calm voice, and chose to support her by inviting her home to eat.

grounding: It shows a teen under results-day pressure coping with rank comparison and parental expectations while keeping her self-worth.
